data.title: Proximity Labeling and Genetic Screening Reveals the Role of DSG2/Siglec-9 Axis in Suppressing Macrophage Phagocytosis
data.projectDescription: In current study, we have established a combined strategy using proximity labeling and genetic screening to identify the cellular ligands of Siglec-9. Our use of proximity labeling using APEX2 fusion proteins followed by quantitative proteomics allowed us to efficiently label and enrich cell surface protein ligands that directly interact with Siglec-9 via sialic acid moieties. By combining with CRISPR knockout screening, we were able to identify functionally significant ligands. We confirmed at the cellular level that DSG2 expressed on cell surfaces directly interacts with Siglec-9, and this interaction is mediated by site-specific N-glycans on the ECD of DGS2. We also demonstrated the binding between DSG2 on A375 melanoma cells and Siglec-9 on macrophages contributes significantly to Siglec-9 signaling and blocking the DSG2-Siglec-9 axis by either DSG2 knockdown or anti-Siglec-9 antibody, releases immune-suppression and increases phagocytosis. Our findings revealed an important ligand in cancer cells for the immunosuppressive receptor Siglec-9, and suggest the potential of disrupting DSG2-Siglec-9 signaling axis in anti-cancer therapy.
data.sampleProcessingProtocol: A375 cells were plated in a 10 cm2 dish at a density of 1×107 cells per plate and incubated overnight at 37 °C in 5% CO2. Following proximity labeling, cells were collected, lysed, enriched with streptavidin magnetic beads, and subjected to on-bead digestion with trypsin protease. For streptavidin enrichment, A375 cells were washed with PBS once, and lysed in lysis buffer consisting of PBS (pH 7.4), 0.1% SDS, 0.1% Trition X-100, 1 mM PMSF, 1 x protease inhibitor cocktail (MCE). Cell lysates were sonicated and cleared by high-speed centrifugation. The protein concentrations were measured by the BSA assay and normalized before enrichment. Each sample was incubated with pre-washed streptavidin magnetic beads (50 μL slurry, MCE) for 2 h at room temperature on a rotator. The streptavidin beads were separated by magnetic rack and sequentially washed with 0.5 mL of 2 M urea in PBS once and 0.5 mL of 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate three times.  For trypsin digestion on beads, the beads were resuspended in 100 μL 50 mM ammonium and transferred into a new 1.5 mL Eppendorf tube. Proteins were reduced and alkylated by the addition of 10 mM dithiothreitol (DTT) and 20 mM iodoacetamide (Sigma Aldrich) and digested with sequence-grade trypsin (Promega) in a final concentration of 10 ng/μL at 37 °C overnight on the shaker at 800 rpm. The supernatant containing the digested peptides was adjusted to pH 2~3 using trifluoroacetic formic acid (TFA), desalted on reverse-phase C18 StageTips (Empore, Sigma) and eluted in 0.1% FA in 50% methanol. The eluted peptide was dried via vacuum centrifugation and stored at -80 °C until LC-MS analysis.
data.dataProcessingProtocol: MS data processing was performed using Proteome Discoverer version 2.4 software (Thermo Fisher Scientific). All raw files were searched with Sequest HT against the proteome database of homo sapiens (202310UP000005640, 82685). The precursor mass tolerance was set to 10 ppm and fragment ion mass tolerance to 0.02 Da. Trypsin was set as the specific proteolytic enzyme, and two missed cleavage site was allowed. Carbamidomethylation (C, +57.02146) was specified as static modifications. Oxidation (M, +15.994915) was specified as a dynamic modification. The target false discovery rate (FDR) of 1% was set for proteins and peptides. Proteins in the inclusion list met the criteria of having at least three unique peptides identified.  Label-free quantification was used for differential proteomic analysis between S9AF- or mS9AF-treated samples. LFQ ratios obtained from Proteome Discoverer were transformed with log2 (x), and P values were obtained using one-way ANOVA test with three technical replicates per sample.
